claims.text: Machine-learning models can accurately predict melting temperature across the HEA family.
Machine-learning models can accurately predict enthalpy and entropy of fusion across the HEA family.
Machine-learning models can accurately predict volume change at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
Machine-learning prediction is an efficient way to determine these HEA properties.
Neural-network or random-forest regression models can use compositional, structural, and thermodynamic descriptors to predict the target properties.
Relevant input features include elemental properties, mixing entropy, atomic-size difference, and thermodynamic parameters.
Accurate application requires a sufficiently large and diverse training dataset.
Model descriptors can capture HEA compositional complexity and atomic-scale disorder.
Machine learning leverages correlations between descriptors and target properties.
These learned correlations permit predictions for new compositions without direct measurement or an ab initio calculation for every composition.
Melting-temperature predictions are expected to have a mean absolute error below 50 K.
Predictions of enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting are expected to have mean absolute errors below 10%.
The proposed prediction errors are comparable to experimental uncertainty.
Direct experimental measurements and first-principles calculations for each alloy are time-consuming and resource-intensive.
The approach is applicable only within the compositional and structural space represented by the training data.
Extrapolation to novel chemistries or extreme conditions may reduce prediction accuracy.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and diversity of the training data.
Limited experimental data for some HEA compositions may constrain model performance.
A mean absolute error above 100 K for melting temperature or above 20% for enthalpy, entropy, or volume change across a held-out test set would falsify the hypothesis.
